questions.topic: Machine Learning Monitoring, Skew, and Drift Detection
questions.question: You are building an ML model to predict customer churn for a subscription service. You have trained your model on GenAI Enterprise Agent Platform using historical data, and deployed it to an Agent Platform endpoint for real-time predictions. After a few weeks, you notice that the model's performance, measured by AUC (area under the ROC curve), has dropped significantly in production compared to its performance during training. How should you troubleshoot this problem?
options: Monitor the latency of the endpoint to determine whether predictions are being generated within the expected time frame.
Use explainable AI tooling to analyze model predictions and understand the impact of each feature on the model's predictions.
Monitor the resource utilization of the endpoint, such as CPU and memory usage, to identify potential bottlenecks in performance.
Monitor the training/serving skew of feature values for requests sent to the endpoint.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: A drop in production AUC compared to training evaluation directly indicates training-serving skew or feature drift. Tracking feature value distributions between training data and serving requests identifies whether data transformation discrepancies or distribution shifts caused the accuracy degradation. Resource and latency metrics measure infrastructure health rather than predictive performance degradation.

questions.topic: Machine Learning Monitoring, Skew, and Drift Detection
questions.question: You maintain a fraud detection model hosted on an Agent Platform endpoint. You trained the model on transaction data from the previous year. Recently, the fraud investigation team reported an increase in false negatives. You suspect that the distribution of new transaction data has shifted significantly compared to the baseline distribution used during training. You need to validate this hypothesis using a managed solution. What should you do?
options: Configure the endpoint to use Model Monitoring. Enable training-serving skew detection, and provide the training dataset as the baseline.
Configure the endpoint to use Model Monitoring. Enable prediction drift detection to compare the current hour's traffic against the previous hour's traffic.
Deploy a new version of the model trained on the same data. Enable feature distribution monitoring in Model Monitoring to track the sampled SHAP values stored for each prediction.

Create a Cloud Logging sink to export the prediction request logs to BigQuery. Write a SQL query to calculate the mean and variance of new features, and compare them to the distribution of the training data.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Vertex AI Model Monitoring natively detects training-serving skew by calculating distance metrics between historical training baseline datasets and live serving payloads. Hourly drift detection compares short-term serving windows against preceding windows rather than the original training baseline. Writing custom SQL queries adds manual overhead when a managed platform feature exists.

questions.topic: Machine Learning Monitoring, Skew, and Drift Detection
questions.question: You work for a large manufacturing company that uses thousands of sensors across its production line. These sensors generate a massive amount of operational data monthly. You have designed an early warning detection model in Agent Platform that monitors for critical machinery and equipment failures. You need to monitor for data and concept drift. You need to assess the model performance given the massive volume of incoming prediction requests. What should you do?
options: Create an additional Agent Platform endpoint. Deploy the model to the new endpoint. Enable robust logging on the endpoint that serves inference assist for critical machinery.
Use Cloud Run functions to trigger the Model Monitoring only during peak production hours estimates to analyze BigQuery data.
Configure the endpoint to log all traffic to BigQuery. Schedule a daily manual evaluation in Agent Platform / custom PyTorch job that analyzes drift in the previous day's data.
Configure a Model Monitoring job for the endpoint. Set the Sample rate to a fraction of the traffic and monitor for feature drift, prediction drift, and model performance.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: For high-throughput streams (petabytes or millions of queries), logging and analyzing 100% of prediction traffic is cost-prohibitive and computationally inefficient. Sampling a representative fraction of serving payloads via Vertex AI Model Monitoring allows continuous drift and skew detection while keeping compute costs minimal.

questions.topic: Machine Learning Monitoring, Skew, and Drift Detection
questions.question: You have deployed a customer churn prediction model to an Agent Platform endpoint. You want to implement a continuous training pipeline that retrains the model when the statistical distribution of the input features in production deviates significantly from the baseline training data. What should you do?
options: Create an Agent Platform Pipelines job that runs on a daily schedule. Include a component that calculates the descriptive statistics of the previous day's production logs and compares them to the training baseline. If deviation is found, the pipeline continues to the retraining component.
Use Agent Platform Experiments to compare the production model AUC vs new AUC over against a later threshold. Trigger a retraining job.
Configure the endpoint to use Model Monitoring to detect training-serving skew. Set an alert to trigger a Pub/Sub that triggers a Cloud Run function to launch the retraining pipeline.

Deploy a new model version alongside the production model using shadow testing. If the new model demonstrates better performance than the production model, automatically promote the new model to replace the old model.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Event-driven architecture is the standard pattern for Continuous Training (CT) in Vertex AI. Model Monitoring continuously evaluates incoming requests. When feature skew or drift exceeds set thresholds, it emits Cloud Monitoring alerts to a Cloud Pub/Sub topic, which triggers a Cloud Run function or Cloud Workflows to launch a Vertex AI Pipeline execution. Detailed Topic Explanation BigQuery ML (BQML) enables operationalizing machine learning directly inside BigQuery using standard SQL queries without exporting data to external frameworks. Time Series Forecasting (ARIMA_PLUS / ARIMA_PLUS_XREG): Designed for demand, sales, and resource forecasting. The ARIMA_PLUS pipeline automatically handles time series modeling tasks, including trend decomposition, seasonality detection (daily, weekly, yearly), holiday effect adjustments, spike/anomaly smoothing, and missing data imputation. Multi-Time Series Forecasting (TIME_SERIES_ID_COL): Allows fitting thousands of distinct time series models (e.g., across multiple warehouse locations or product SKUs) in a single CREATE MODEL statement. Feature Transformation (TRANSFORM clause): Preprocessing functions embedded directly inside the CREATE MODEL definition. Features specified in TRANSFORM are automatically stored as part of the model object and applied consistently during ML.PREDICT or ML.FORECAST execution. Real-Life Example A nationwide logistics vendor needs to forecast daily shipped packages across 500 distinct regional warehouses. Instead of extracting data out of BigQuery into custom Python scripts, building 500 separate Prophet or ARIMA pipelines, and managing feature extraction scripts: SQL Native Execution: A single CREATE MODEL statement uses TIME_SERIES_ID_COL='warehouse_id' and TIME_SERIES_TIMESTAMP_COL='shipment_date'. Automated Preprocessing: BQML builds 500 individual ARIMA_PLUS sub-models in parallel. It handles missing records, removes outlier spikes from sudden weather delays, incorporates local holiday calendars, and outputs future demand predictions using ML.FORECAST. How to Work With BQML ARIMA_PLUS Step 1: Create the Forecasting Model Run a SQL statement in BigQuery Studio to build multi-time-series models across multiple entities. SQL CREATE OR REPLACE MODEL `my_project.inventory.warehouse_forecast_model` OPTIONS( MODEL_TYPE = 'ARIMA_PLUS', TIME_SERIES_TIMESTAMP_COL = 'shipment_date', TIME_SERIES_DATA_COL = 'total_packages', TIME_SERIES_ID_COL = 'warehouse_id', HOLIDAY_REGION = 'US', AUTO_ARIMA = TRUE ) AS SELECT warehouse_id, shipment_date, total_packages FROM `my_project.inventory.daily_shipment`; Step 2: Generate Predictions via SQL Forecast future values over a horizon period (e.g., 30 days) using ML.FORECAST. SQL SELECT * FROM ML.FORECAST( MODEL `my_project.inventory.warehouse_forecast_model`, STRUCT(30 AS horizon, 0.95 AS confidence_level) ); Categorized Exam Questions

questions.topic: BigQuery ML, Time Series Forecasting (ARIMA_PLUS), and Data Engineering
questions.question: You work for a logistics company. You have a BigQuery table named daily_shipment. This table contains historical data with three columns: warehouse_id, shipment_date, and total_packages. You want to create a model that uses SQL to forecast the daily total_packages for each warehouse_id. You want the solution to automatically detect and account for data anomalies, holidays, and seasonality without requiring manual feature engineering. What should you do?
options: Use the CREATE MODEL statement with model_type='ARIMA_PLUS_XREG'. Generate the forecast using the ML.FORECAST command.

Use the CREATE MODEL statement with model_type='ARIMA_PLUS', TIME_SERIES_DATA_COL option and shipment_date in the TIME_SERIES_TIMESTAMP_COL option, alongside TIME_SERIES_ID_COL='warehouse_id'. Generate the forecast using the ML.FORECAST command.
Use the CREATE MODEL statement with model_type='ARIMA_PLUS'. Scale the total_packages column using ML.BUCKETIZE. Generate the forecast using the ML.PREDICT command.
Use the CREATE MODEL statement with model_type='ARIMA_PLUS'. Scale the total_packages column and add holiday logic manually. Generate the forecast using the ML.FORECAST command.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: ARIMA_PLUS automatically performs anomaly detection, seasonal adjustments, and holiday incorporation. Using TIME_SERIES_ID_COL trains distinct time series models for every unique warehouse_id inside the table. Predictions are generated via ML.FORECAST.

questions.question: You are in the exploratory phase of development of a demand forecasting model. Several terabytes of historical sales data are stored in a BigQuery table. You need to create a new, clean table to perform preliminary analysis on metrics, such as monthly sales figures and weekly aggregates, without additional data movement. You want to use the simplest approach and minimize overhead. What should you do?
options: Write a SQL query in the BigQuery console. Use standard SQL functions like CAST, EXTRACT, and window functions with GROUP BY clauses to perform the transformations and calculations. Materialize the results into a new destination table in BigQuery.

Read the data from BigQuery into a Dask DataFrame using Agent Platform Workbench. Perform exploratory data analysis (EDA) and feature engineering transformations, and write the processed data back to a new destination table in BigQuery.

Write a SQL query in the BigQuery console. Use the ML.TRANSFORM function in BigQuery ML to compute the moving averages and extract time-based features. Write the processed data to a new destination table in BigQuery.
Create a PreprocessingOp component in the Agent Platform Pipelines workflow to compute the moving averages and time-based features and write the processed data to a new destination table in BigQuery.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Data is already in BigQuery. Using standard SQL directly inside BigQuery processes terabytes in seconds using serverless compute without moving data across network boundaries or creating pipelines. ML.TRANSFORM is designed for pre-preprocessing inside CREATE MODEL definitions, not for generating standalone exploratory tables.

questions.question: You are the lead ML engineer for a large ecommerce company. The Data Analytics team has prepared a dataset with millions of transaction rows stored in a partitioned BigQuery table. The team consists primarily of SQL experts with limited experience in Python or TensorFlow. You need to build a binary classification model to predict customer purchases. You need to provide daily batch predictions while minimizing development effort, data movement, and overall complexity. What should you do?
options: Create a model with BigQuery ML that includes MODEL_TYPE='AUTOML_CLASSIFIER'. Use the ML.PREDICT function to generate predictions as part of your nightly data warehouse jobs.
Use the BigQuery ML TRANSFORM function to normalize features and train a MODEL_TYPE='LOGISTIC_REG' model. Use ML.PREDICT for predictions.
Train a classification model with Agent Platform AutoML Tabular Workflows, deploy to an endpoint, and use Cloud Run for batch predictions.
Develop an XGBoost model on an Agent Platform Workbench notebook. Load data into pandas DataFrames, pickle it to Cloud Storage, and schedule the notebook.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: MODEL_TYPE='AUTOML_CLASSIFIER' in BigQuery ML leverages Vertex AI AutoML capabilities directly inside SQL. This keeps all data inside BigQuery, avoids data egress, requires zero Python code, and integrates directly into nightly SQL batch scheduling. Detailed Topic Explanation Machine learning models rely on high-quality features, but online inference and offline training often require features computed at different time steps. Training-Serving Skew in Features: If an online model uses feature values updated in real time, but offline training joins historical logs with the current feature values, the model learns from "future" data (data leakage). Point-in-Time (Time-Travel) Lookup: Vertex AI Feature Store allows running point-in-time joins. Given a list of entity IDs and historical timestamps, Feature Store fetches the exact feature values present at those specific moments in history. Streaming Feature Ingestion: Apache Beam / Dataflow pipelines process continuous real-time events (e.g., from Pub/Sub) and write aggregated metrics (like 1-hour transaction counts) directly to Feature Store for ultra-low latency online serving. Real-Life Example A credit card provider evaluates fraud risk in real time. One key feature is count_transactions_last_1_hour. At Online Inference: The model queries Vertex AI Feature Store to get the current value of count_transactions_last_1_hour for a customer attempting a transaction at 2:15 PM. At Offline Retraining: For a transaction that occurred three months ago at 10:00 AM, the training pipeline must look up what count_transactions_last_1_hour was at 10:00 AM three months ago, not what it is today. A point-in-time lookup fetches this historical snapshot automatically. How to Work With Vertex AI Feature Store Point-in-Time Lookups Step 1: Define Your Entity Observations Table in BigQuery Create a table containing the entity IDs and the historical timestamps for training. SQL SELECT user_id, transaction_time, is_fraud FROM `my_project.fraud.historical_transactions` Step 2: Trigger Point-in-Time Batch Serving via Python SDK Python from google.cloud import aiplatform aiplatform.init(project="my-project", location="us-central1") entity_type = aiplatform.Featurestore("projects/12345/locations/us-central1/featurestores/fraud_fs"). entity_types["user"] # Run point-in-time lookup entity_type.batch_read_feature_values( destination_table_uri="bq://my_project.fraud.training_dataset", feature_selector=["count_transactions_last_1_hour", "avg_amount_30_days"], entity_type_specs=[ { "entity_type_id": "user", "bq_source_uri": "bq://my_project.fraud.historical_transactions", "feature_ids": ["count_transactions_last_1_hour", "avg_amount_30_days"] } ] ) Categorized Exam Questions

questions.topic: Feature Store, Point-in-Time Joins, and Dataflow Streaming
questions.question: You are designing an Agent Platform Pipelines workflow for a real-time credit card fraud detection model. The model relies on dynamic features that change frequently, such as "number of transactions in the last hour," which you calculate continuously in Agent Platform Feature Store. You are preparing the training dataset using historical transaction logs. You need to ensure that the feature values associated with the historical transaction in the training set accurately reflect the user state at the time of the transaction. You want to use the simplest approach. What should you do?
options: Configure the pipeline to run a batch serving job from Agent Platform Feature Store. Point the job to the transaction IDs and their timestamps to perform a point-in-time lookup to create the training dataset.

Configure the pipeline to export the current feature values from Agent Platform Feature Store to BigQuery. Write a SQL query to join those values with the historical transaction logs to create the training dataset.

Create a Dataflow pipeline that ingests the historical transaction logs, groups them by user, and calculates the new aggregated statistics. Store the results in Cloud Storage for the training pipeline to consume.

Create a Dataflow pipeline that reads the historical transaction logs. For each transaction, configure the pipeline to query the Agent Platform Feature Store online serving to retrieve the feature values. Join the feature values with the transaction data to create the training dataset.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Point-in-time lookup is a managed capability of Vertex AI Feature Store designed specifically to prevent data leakage in time-series training data. It fetches feature values matching the historical transaction timestamp without manual joins or building complex custom data processing scripts.

questions.question: Your team is deploying a real-time personalized recommendation model. The model requires low-latency access for hundreds of raw features to be fetched at request time. These features are stored in BigQuery and updated frequently by a streaming pipeline. As your team continues to grow, you discover that fetching features from BigQuery at request time is causing the total latency during serving to exceed your 100 ms SLA. You need to process concurrent retrieval automatically while minimizing operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Use BigQuery BI Engine to accelerate the SQL queries used to fetch features.
Enable Agent Platform Feature Store, and use the Feature Store API to fetch features.
Use the BigQuery Storage / Feature Store Client to stream data directly from the model inference cluster.
Implement a Redis cache on Memorystore and add a component to the solution monitoring to sync with the feature store on the fly.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Vertex AI Feature Store provides a low-latency, high-throughput online serving layer optimized for sub-100ms real-time inference calls. Querying analytical data warehouses like BigQuery directly during online inference introduces unacceptable latency.

questions.question: You work in the credit card fraud detection department of a bank that processes millions of transactions per day. You need to create and serve a real-time fraud detection model. To address the challenge of feature engineering at this scale with limited raw data, you plan to create time-related aggregate features, such as the average transaction amount within the last month or the amount of time since the last transaction. How should you process the data for model training and serving?
options: Ingest the transaction data into BigQuery. Use a TRANSFORM model in BigQuery ML to create a reusable feature engineering pipeline.
Orchestrate a workflow in Agent Platform Pipelines that exports raw transaction data from BigQuery to Cloud Storage. Perform feature engineering using a Python script in a custom component.
Ingest the transaction data into BigQuery. Use the TRANSFORM clause in BigQuery ML to create new features by applying SQL functions to the raw transaction data.

Create streaming Dataflow pipelines that read transaction data from Pub/Sub. Use a windowing function to aggregate transaction data over time. Store the engineered features in Agent Platform Feature Store.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Real-time fraud detection requires continuously updated streaming aggregate features (e.g., sliding 1-hour or 30-day windows). Dataflow natively handles streaming window aggregations from Pub/Sub, and writing the computed aggregates into Vertex AI Feature Store makes them immediately available for low-latency online inference. Detailed Topic Explanation Deploying Generative AI applications at enterprise scale requires balancing model capability with cost, latency, safety, and operational control: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vs. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): RAG grounds foundational models with dynamic internal knowledge (e.g., PDF documentation, databases) to eliminate hallucinations and reflect daily updates without retraining. SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) is ideal when the model must learn specific output styles, specialized syntax (e.g., internal code constructs), or structured behaviors. Explicit Context Caching: When sending large, static reference materials (e.g., manuals or multiple enterprise PDFs) in context windows repeatedly, Explicit Context Caching stores preprocessed tokens in memory. This reduces latency and input token costs by up to 80% for high-volume repeat queries. Model Armor & Sensitive Data Protection: Model Armor acts as an inline AI firewall to intercept and screen prompts and responses against jailbreak attacks, prompt injections, and toxic content before or after reaching the LLM. Integrated with Sensitive Data Protection (DLP), it scans for and de-identifies Personally Identifiable Information (PII). AutoSxS (Automatic Side-by-Side): A fully managed pipeline component that acts as an "LLM-as-a-judge" to evaluate and score two model versions automatically based on specific evaluation criteria. Real-Life Example A commercial bank builds a customer service chatbot. Context Caching & RAG: The bank's 500-page policy document is stored in Cloud Storage. Instead of sending the full document with every API request, the system creates an Explicit Context Cache. User questions about interest rates are served instantly with lower latency and cheaper token fees. Model Armor & PII Filtering: When a user asks a question containing their credit card or social security number, Model Armor with Sensitive Data Protection automatically redacts the sensitive PII before passing the prompt to the model and scrubs any private details from the generated output. AutoSxS Evaluation: Before deploying a fine-tuned Gemini model to replace an existing baseline model, the team runs an AutoSxS evaluation pipeline to systematically score response quality. How to Work With Explicit Context Caching in Python Step 1: Create an Explicit Context Cache for Large Static Documents Python import datetime from google import genai from google.genai import types client = genai.Client(project="my-project", location="us-central1") # Create explicit cache with a 7-day Time-To-Live (TTL) cache = client.caches.create( model="gemini-1.5-pro", config=types.CreateCachedContentConfig( contents=[ types.Part.from_uri( file_uri="gs://my-bucket/company_policy_manual.pdf", mime_type="application/pdf" ) ], ttl=datetime.timedelta(days=7), ) ) print(f"Cache created: {cache.name}") Step 2: Generate Content Using the Cached Context Python response = client.models.generate_content( model="gemini-1.5-pro", contents="What is the policy for international wire transfers?", config=types.GenerateContentConfig( cached_content=cache.name ) ) print(response.text) Categorized Exam Questions

questions.question: Your organization's employee onboarding team wants you to build an interactive self-help app for new employees. The app needs to answer queries from users and provide answers from the organization's internal documentation. This documentation is stored across various documents such as PDF files. You want to build a solution quickly while minimizing maintenance overhead. What should you do?
options: Deploy an internal website to a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Build a search index for the organization's internal documentation. Use Vector Search to implement a semantic search that retrieves results from the search index based on the query entered into the search box.

Create a custom chatbot user interface hosted on App Engine. Use Agent Platform or fine-tune a Gemini model on the organization's internal documentation. Send users' queries to the fine-tuned model by using the custom chatbot and return the model's responses to the users.

Deploy an internal website to a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Organize the relevant internal documentation into sections. Collect user feedback on website content and store in BigQuery. Recalculate the embeddings and regularly update the links based on user feedback.

Use Agent Search to create an agent. Securely index the organization's internal documentation to the agent's datastore. Send users' queries to the agent and return the agent's grounded responses to the users.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Vertex AI Search (Agent Search) is a fully managed out-of-the-box solution designed specifically for turn-key document indexing and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). It ingests unorganized PDF documentation directly with minimal setup, eliminating the need to manage infrastructure like GKE, custom vector stores, or application hosting code.

questions.question: Your team is experimenting with fine-tuning smaller, distilled LLMs for a specific domain. You have performed batch inference and are evaluating using two variations of your distilled LLMs and stored the batch inference outputs in Cloud Storage. You need to create an evaluation workflow that integrates with your existing pipeline in Agent Platform. You need to assess the performance of the LLM versions while you are rapidly iterating. What should you do?
options: Create a custom Agent Platform Pipelines component that reads the batch inference outputs from Cloud Storage, calculates evaluation metrics, and writes the results to a BigQuery table.

Use the automatic side-by-side (AutoSxS) Agent Platform Pipelines component that performs the batch inference evaluation from Cloud Storage, aggregates evaluation metrics, and writes the results to a BigQuery table.
Develop a custom component that reads the batch inference outputs from Cloud Storage, calculates evaluation metrics as a distributed runner, and writes the results to a BigQuery table.
Use a Dataflow component that processes the batch inference outputs from Cloud Storage, calculates evaluation metrics as a distributed runner, and writes the results to a BigQuery table.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: AutoSxS is a managed Vertex AI Pipelines component designed to evaluate two LLM outputs side-by-side using an LLM-as-a-judge. It eliminates writing custom evaluation scripts and integrates directly with pipeline artifacts stored in Google Cloud Storage and BigQuery.

questions.question: You are developing a Gemini-based onboarding chatbot to answer users' questions based on five PDFs encompassing information in Cloud Storage. The documents are updated weekly or monthly as needed. You expect that the application will receive high-volume, repeated queries against this documentation context. You need to use the most appropriate and cost-effective solution for managing the context and ensuring low latency for end-user information. What should you do?
options: Fine-tune a Gemini model using the text from the five PDF files as a training dataset.
Send requests with the five PDF files as content pointing to the URI file. Use implicit context caching.
Create an explicit context cache using the five PDF files, and regenerate the cache when the source files are updated.
Create an explicit context cache using the five PDF files. Set a time-to-live (TTL) of seven days, and regenerate the cache when source files change.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Explicit context caching is specifically designed for scenarios where the same large static context (e.g., reference PDFs) is reused across high-volume requests. Regenerating the explicit cache only when source files are modified guarantees high response speeds and lower input token costs.

questions.question: Your team is developing a customer support chatbot for a healthcare company that processes sensitive patient information. You need to ensure that all personally identifiable information (PII) captured during customer conversations is protected prior to storing or analyzing the data. What should you do?
options: Use the Cloud Natural Language API to identify and redact PII in chatbot conversations.
Use the Cloud Natural Language API to classify and categorize all data, including PII, in chatbot conversations.
Use the DLP API to encrypt PII in chatbot conversations before storing the data.
Use the DLP API to scan and de-identify PII in chatbot conversations before storing the data.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud DLP API) is Google Cloud's dedicated service for discovering, scanning, and de-identifying (masking, redacting, tokenizing) PII in unstructured text. Natural Language API is intended for sentiment and syntactic analysis, not privacy masking.

questions.question: Your work for a media company that offers a news service. News articles are currently manually assigned multiple tags based on their content. You need to create a scalable solution that accurately and automatically tags articles. You have a historical dataset of 1 million articles with 120 distinct tags in a Cloud Storage bucket. Your team has limited experience with LLMs but has programming skills. What should you do?
options: Import data to BigQuery, and apply the Gemini LLM API to the database. Insert multiple auto-tagging batch in the current model.
Use the Natural Language API to perform entity recognition directly on its Cloud Storage database. Use the extracted entities as tags.
Import data to BigQuery, and fine-tune the Gemini model from Model Garden using the dataset to customize it for tagging.
Fine-tune the Gemini model from Model Garden using Vertex AI Workbench notebook. Use the fine-tuned model for tagging directly on the Cloud Storage dataset.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: With 120 distinct domain-specific tags and 1 million examples, fine-tuning an LLM adapts the model to output precise tags matching internal business definitions. Ingesting data into BigQuery allows managed supervised fine-tuning directly through Vertex AI or BigQuery ML without manual training infrastructure management.

questions.question: You are orchestrating a continuous deployment pipeline in Agent Platform Pipelines for a fine-tuned Gemini model that summarizes complex legal documents. Before deploying each new model version to production, you need to systematically evaluate its summarization quality against the current production model. You want to use an automated, scalable approach that uses an LLM-as-judge and determine which model produces better summaries based on specific criteria. What should you do?
options: Add a custom Python component that generates predictions from both models. Calculate the BLEU or ROUGE-L scores between the generated summaries and a golden dataset.

Integrate the Model Evaluation (classification) component into the pipeline. Configure the evaluation task as the summarization tokens as a multi-class classification problem, and calculate the perplexity score.
Add the automatic side-by-side (AutoSxS) pipeline component to your workflow. Configure the component to use the autorater service to score the responses of both models and compare their results.
Use the Gen AI evaluation service to run a standalone experiment comparing the responses of both models in an Agent Platform Colab Enterprise notebook.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: AutoSxS uses an automated autorater (LLM-as-a-judge) component natively inside Vertex AI Pipelines. Standard NLP metrics like BLEU or ROUGE measure surface token overlap rather than semantic summarization quality, making AutoSxS the best scalable approach.

Run the model evaluation service. Configure the job to use adversarial testing to identify jailbreak attempts and determine the model's refusal rate.

Create an Agent Platform batch prediction job using a dataset of historical jailbreak prompts. Analyze the outputs manually to calculate the percentage of responses blocked by the Agent Platform safety filters.
Deploy the model to an Agent Platform endpoint behind Model Armor. Review the Cloud Logging entries generated by Model Armor to identify which incoming requests trigger the jailbreak filter.

questions.question: You have created a prototype of a real-time customer support virtual agent using Gemini Pro that has achieved great results. During load testing, you discover that the cost per query and the end-user latency are higher than expected. You need to reduce both cost and latency while maintaining high-quality responses. What should you do?
options: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the Gemini Pro model to reserve dedicated compute resources.
Re-engineer the virtual agent to use Gemini Flash to classify the user's intent. Answer simple queries using Gemini Flash, and route more complex queries to Gemini Pro.
Batch incoming user queries into groups of 15 before processing them with Gemini Pro.

questions.question: You recently developed an internal custom RAG solution. The application performed well in a development environment on a set of PDF documents. However, after productionizing the application across your entire organization, model performance has degraded significantly. You need to maximize the solution's response accuracy and scalability. What should you do?
options: Disable context caching in the Gemini API.
Split the RAG into smaller domain-specific architectures, and integrate them with a unified framework solution.
Migrate the matching engine to Vector Search.
Migrate your raw data to Datastore, and increase the chunk size.
questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: When scaling a RAG system from a handful of documents to enterprise scale, basic flat vector matching or in-memory vector indexing fails in both retrieval precision and query latency. Migrating the indexing and vector retrieval layer to Vertex AI Vector Search (formerly Matching Engine) provides enterprise-grade Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search across millions of embeddings with millisecond retrieval performance. Detailed Topic Explanation Deploying machine learning models for production inference on Google Cloud requires choosing the right balance between simplicity, customization, latency, and hardware acceleration: Custom Prediction Routines (CPR) vs. Custom Containers: When deploying custom frameworks (such as scikit-learn or PyTorch) that require preprocessing logic (e.g., image resizing, tokenization) alongside model evaluation: CPR: Provides a managed Python abstraction where developers write a simple Predictor class containing preprocess(), predict(), and postprocess() methods. Vertex AI builds and packages the container automatically. Custom Containers: Full Docker container control required for non-standard OS-level binaries, C++ dependencies, or complete control over execution environments. Endpoint Autoscaling Dynamics: Vertex AI Endpoint autoscaling scales replicas based on CPU or GPU metrics. If GPU usage is 90%+ while CPU is <40%, CPU-based autoscaling will fail to trigger new replicas, causing latency spikes. Autoscaling rules must monitor the bottleneck metric (GPU Duty Cycle). To prevent service degradation during sudden traffic spikes (e.g., flash sales jump from 1k to 50k QPS), min_replica_count must be set to a high baseline capacity to avoid initial cold-start autoscaling lag. Hardware Acceleration Strategies: Data Parallelism: Replicates model parameters across multiple GPUs/TPUs, splitting input data batches. Ideal when the model easily fits into individual GPU VRAM. Model/Pipeline Parallelism: Shards large model parameters (e.g., 70B–100B+ parameter LLMs) across the VRAM of multiple GPUs/TPUs when a single GPU suffers Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. Real-Life Example A retail application deploys a deep learning image classification model on a Vertex AI endpoint backed by NVIDIA GPUs. Pre/Post-Processing: Incoming HTTP requests send raw base64 image bytes. Instead of forcing client applications to resize images locally, the team uses a Custom Prediction Routine (CPR). The server-side preprocess() function decodes and normalizes images directly before running inference. Autoscaling Adjustment: During load testing, traffic increases caused 503 latency timeouts even though endpoint CPU usage stayed low. Engineers discovered the GPU was at 95% capacity while CPU stayed at 30%. Updating autoscaling target metrics to track GPU Duty Cycle resolved scaling bottlenecks. How to Work With Vertex AI Custom Prediction Routines (CPR) Step 1: Define Custom Predictor Class Python import os import pickle import numpy as np from google.cloud.aiplatform.prediction import Predictor class CustomTextPredictor(Predictor): def init (self): self._model = None def load(self, artifacts_uri: str) -> None: """Loads model artifacts from Cloud Storage.""" model_path = os.path.join(artifacts_uri, "model.pkl") with open(model_path, "rb") as f: self._model = pickle.load(f) def preprocess(self, prediction_input: dict) -> np.ndarray: """Transforms raw input JSON into normalized arrays.""" instances = prediction_input["instances"] # Custom preprocessing logic (e.g., lowercasing, feature extraction) processed_data = np.array([text.lower().split() for text in instances]) return processed_data def predict(self, instances: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """Runs inference.""" return self._model.predict(instances) def postprocess(self, prediction_results: np.ndarray) -> dict: """Formats output response.""" return {"predictions": prediction_results.tolist()} Step 2: Build and Deploy using Vertex AI SDK Python from google.cloud import aiplatform from google.cloud.aiplatform.prediction import LocalModel # Package custom predictor into a local container artifact local_model = LocalModel.build_cpr_model( src_dir="src/", output_image_uri="gcr.io/my-project/custom-predictor:v1", predictor=CustomTextPredictor, requirements_path="requirements.txt" ) # Upload and deploy to Vertex AI Endpoint local_model.push_image() model = aiplatform.Model.upload( display_name="custom-cpr-model", serving_container_image_uri="gcr.io/my-project/custom-predictor:v1", artifact_uri="gs://my-bucket/model-artifacts/" ) endpoint = model.deploy(machine_type="n1-standard-4", min_replica_count=2) Categorized Exam Questions

You need to implement server-side logic to decode bytes, resize images, and normalize pixels before passing them to the model. You want to minimize latency and operational overhead. questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: CPR abstracts container creation, health endpoints, and HTTP routing while providing a structured Python class interface (preprocess, predict, postprocess). It reduces operational overhead compared to writing custom FastAPI web servers or proxy microservices. Detailed Topic Explanation Constructing production-grade machine learning systems requires automated orchestration pipelines to manage training, validation, deployment, and continuous retraining (CT): Orchestration Frameworks: Vertex AI Pipelines: Uses the Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) SDK. It provides serverless execution of containerized ML steps with built-in artifact tracking, execution caching, and lineage management. Cloud Composer (Managed Apache Airflow): Preferred when orchestrating multi-cloud workflows, complex hybrid environments, or non-ML platform dependencies (e.g., executing on-premises shell scripts alongside cloud triggers). Triggers & Event-Driven Automation: Daily / Scheduled Retraining: Cloud Scheduler calls a lightweight trigger function (e.g., Cloud Run or Cloud Functions) to submit a compiled Vertex AI Pipeline JSON definition on a cron schedule. Event-Based / Data Ingestion Triggers: Cloud Storage bucket triggers pass newly uploaded data notifications directly to Cloud Run functions to start pipeline runs. Code-Based Triggers (CI/CD): Cloud Build monitors code repositories (e.g., GitHub). When pipeline code or Docker container logic changes on the main branch, Cloud Build builds new container images, pushes them to Artifact Registry, compiles the new pipeline specification, and uploads it to Cloud Storage. Model Registry Aliases for Zero-Downtime Deployment: Batch inference pipelines and production serving applications reference model aliases (e.g., production) rather than hardcoded model version IDs. Promoting a new, retrained model simply involves reassigning the production alias to the new version in Model Registry, instantly routing downstream batch jobs without application code modifications. Real-Life Example A logistics company maintains a daily freight demand model. CI/CD Pipeline: A data scientist updates the training component logic and merges code to Git. Cloud Build automatically triggers, builds a new Docker image containing updated dependencies, pushes it to Artifact Registry, compiles the pipeline into JSON, and saves it in Cloud Storage. Scheduled Execution: Every night at 2:00 AM, Cloud Scheduler triggers a Cloud Run service that submits the latest compiled pipeline JSON to Vertex AI Pipelines. Safe Promotion: The pipeline validates the new model's performance. If validation metrics pass, the pipeline updates the production alias in Vertex AI Model Registry. How to Work With Vertex AI Pipelines & Caching Step 1: Define a Kubeflow Pipeline with Caching Enabled Python from kfp import dsl from google.cloud import aiplatform @dsl.component(base_image="python:3.10") def preprocess_op(input_path: str) -> str: # Heavy data preprocessing logic output_path = input_path.replace(".csv", "_processed.csv") return output_path @dsl.component(base_image="python:3.10") def train_op(processed_data_path: str) -> str: # Model training logic return "gs://my-bucket/models/model.pkl" @dsl.pipeline( name="retraining-pipeline", pipeline_root="gs://my-bucket/pipeline_root" ) def my_pipeline(data_uri: str): # Enable caching: runs only if input parameters or logic changed prep_task = preprocess_op(input_path=data_uri) prep_task.set_caching_options(enable_caching=True) train_task = train_op(processed_data_path=prep_task.output) # Compile pipeline to JSON from kfp import compiler compiler.Compiler().compile( pipeline_func=my_pipeline, package_path="pipeline_spec.json" ) Step 2: Submit Job via Cloud Run / Python SDK Python job = aiplatform.PipelineJob( display_name="scheduled-retrain-run", template_path="pipeline_spec.json", parameter_values={"data_uri": "gs://my-bucket/data.csv"}, enable_caching=True ) job.submit() Categorized Exam Questions

questions.explanation: Technical Explanation: Vertex AI Pipelines features built-in execution caching. When caching is enabled (enable_caching=True), the execution engine checks if a previous component execution exists with the exact same code, inputs, and parameters. If found, it skips execution and reuses the cached output artifacts, saving execution time and compute costs. Detailed Topic Explanation When building enterprise ML applications, custom model development isn't always optimal or cost-effective. Google Cloud provides pre-trained, managed ML services for domain-specific tasks: Document AI: Purpose-built for extracting structured data from unstructured documents (e.g., invoices, receipts, tax forms, procurement contracts). It uses Specialized Processors (like the Invoice Processor) that combine OCR, spatial layout analysis, and NLP to output structured JSON entities automatically. Vision API & Cloud Natural Language API: Vision API: Ideal for general optical character recognition (TEXT_DETECTION), explicit content detection (SAFE_SEARCH_DETECTION), object detection, and image labeling. Natural Language API: Optimized for entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and syntax parsing on raw unstructured text. Vertex AI Search (Agent Search) & Layout Parser: Used when you need semantic search or RAG across unstructured enterprise documents (PDFs, docs) with minimal manual parsing, vector indexing, or pipeline maintenance. Real-Life Example A global accounts payable team receives 10,000 PDF invoices daily from hundreds of vendors, each with different layouts. Bad Approach: Writing complex Regex scripts over Cloud Vision OCR outputs or training a custom Named Entity Recognition (NER) model from scratch. Best Approach: Routing incoming PDFs to Document AI's Invoice Processor. It accurately extracts key fields—such as invoice_id, total_amount, line_items, and due_date—regardless of template layout changes, outputting structured data directly into BigQuery. How to Work With Document AI (Python SDK) Python from google.cloud import documentai_v1 as documentai def process_invoice(project_id: str, location: str, processor_id: str, file_path: str): client = documentai.DocumentProcessorServiceClient() name = client.processor_path(project_id, location, processor_id) with open(file_path, "rb") as image: image_content = image.read() raw_document = documentai.RawDocument(content=image_content, mime_type="application/pdf") request = documentai.ProcessRequest(name=name, raw_document=raw_document) result = client.process_document(request=request) document = result.document # Print extracted entities for entity in document.entities: print(f"Entity: {entity.type_} -> {entity.mention_text}") Categorized Exam Questions

Detailed Topic Explanation Training modern large language models, computer vision networks, and diffusion models requires selecting the appropriate hardware acceleration and memory optimization techniques: NVIDIA GPUs vs. Google Cloud TPUs: GPUs (e.g., A100, B200, T4): General-purpose accelerators supported across all frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX). Preferred for custom open-source libraries, CUDA dependencies, and standard ML models. TPUs (v4, v5e, v5p): Google-custom ASIC hardware built specifically for matrix multiplication at extreme scale. Ideal for large foundation model pre-training/fine-tuning (JAX/TensorFlow/PyTorch) across pod slices. Precision and Quantization Techniques: Mixed Precision (bf16 / fp16): Uses 16-bit floating-point numbers for matrix math while preserving 32-bit (fp32) master weights. Drastically cuts memory footprint and doubles training throughput without loss of model accuracy. DataLoader Optimization (num_workers & pin_memory): When GPU memory utilization fluctuates (drops to 0% continuously while CPU utilization stays >90%), the GPU is data-starved waiting for the CPU to load and decode input batches. Increasing num_workers in PyTorch's DataLoader and enabling pin_memory=True resolves CPU input bottlenecks. Real-Life Example An ML engineer notices an NVIDIA A100 GPU running a custom PyTorch image training job has volatile GPU usage—it regularly spikes to 100% then drops to 0% for several seconds while CPU utilization remains pegged at 95%. Diagnosis: The GPU finishes computing matrix gradients in milliseconds, but must pause because the CPU main thread is stuck reading image files off storage and performing disk I/O synchronously. Fix: In the PyTorch script, set num_workers=8 (to use multi-threaded background data fetching) and pin_memory=True (to stage tensors in fast host RAM). GPU utilization stabilizes near 100%.
